question_notes.1093: KNOWN-UNSTABLE ITEM (accepted as such 2026-09-02). Question: the S4E4 title of a series whose S4 was released 2007-2017, whose S4E4 director made their directorial debut 1991-2001, whose creator co-wrote a sitcom aired 1996-2006, and with a character born 1992-2000. Gold: 'Hang the DJ' (Black Mirror S4E4). The gold chain IS in the corpus and was verified end-to-end (34407.md series_no 4 / episode 4 / director Tim Van Patten / release 2017-12-29; 62349.md Tim Van Patten 'made his directorial film debut ... in 1991' with an '1991-2001: Early directing work' section heading; 87905.md Nathan Barley sitcom by Chris Morris and Charlie Brooker; 12171.md Charlie Brooker 'creator ... of Black Mirror' + 'co-wrote the sitcom Nathan Barley'; 36200.md Georgina Campbell 'born 12 June 1992'). Verdict oscillates across identical configurations: run 2026-09-01 23:05 (v8) scored level 4 with 'Final Answer: **Hang the DJ**', while runs v9/v10/v11/v13/v14 (2026-09-02) scored level 0, guessing Bob's Burgers 'My Big Fat Greek Bob', Glee 'The Break-Up', or Game of Thrones 'Oathkeeper' - all of which satisfy only the creator/sitcom constraint. ROOT CAUSE (located at query-string level): the model's constraint queries still NAME the candidate it already has (e.g. 'Bernard Derriman directorial debut | ... | Bob's Burgers.*Derriman | My Big Fat Greek Bob.*Derriman'), so retrieval can never surface the Black Mirror family (Tim Van Patten / Nathan Barley / Charlie Brooker). Whether the correct family is ever reached is decided by whether an early candidate-enumeration query happens to hit it, which is why the outcome is non-deterministic. Gate/auditor behaviour is healthy (audits 8-16 rounds, no crashes, no context-limit failures since patch 17/19/24/26); this is a recall-stability limit, not a pipeline defect. Detailed analysis: tasks/2026-09-02-q1093-analysis.md.

history._fix_priority_20260915: FIX PRIORITY between the two big failure buckets, measured on the browsecomp_retry_batch run (2026-09-15). KEY FINDING: `failed_retrieval_strategy` is MISNAMED - it is not a retrieval-backend limitation. The reachability probe (outputs/reachability_20260914_134349, BM25 at doc level, top-30) shows 18 of its 25 questions reach an expected doc at rank 1-7 using the GOLD NAME, and 3 more (q26/q856/q869) reach one using the QUESTION'S OWN WORDING (rank 7/16/16). Yet 0 of the 25 runs ever issued a query containing the gold entity, and only 1/25 retrieved an expected doc. The blocker is query vocabulary / hypothesis generation - we cannot search a name we never generate - not the index. By contrast `failed_evidence_in_hand` is a selection/discipline failure: 13/20 runs had an expected doc in their own retrieved_docids and 14/20 are on record as having READ a doc containing the gold string, yet shipped a different value. So: attack evidence_in_hand first (a rule at the gate, applies to all 830 questions, at the historical 39/89 = 44% failure-fix rate ~8-9 of the 20 should flip, with the precedent of zero regressions); then chase q26/q856/q869 as a MECHANICAL bug (the question's own words hit rank 7-16 and 119-132 queries never got there - check whether the rare question tokens were ever queried and whether the top-k/similarity cutoff drops a rank-16 hit); only then invest in the generic capability the retr bucket really needs - mining candidate entity names out of the read neighbourhood and back-searching each name, which is the highest-leverage change (18/25 are one name away) but a capability increment rather than a rule. RETRACTION: an earlier cut of this analysis claimed 100% of both buckets had `expected_doc_ids` inside `answers.jsonl:evidence_doc_ids`. That field is a DATASET INPUT (in questions.jsonl evidence_doc_ids is a superset of expected_doc_ids for 830/830 questions), so it says nothing about what the run had in hand; it must not be used as a runtime signal. The valid signals are the run's own retrieved_docids and the per-question notes.
history._evidence_in_hand_diagnosis_20260915: WHY evidence_in_hand FAILS, measured 2026-09-15 on browsecomp_retry_batch (answers.jsonl + agentic_rag.yaml). The adjudication rules the class was assumed to need ALREADY EXIST in the answer_auditor: `suspect: answer value appears in no cited evidence` (line 371, plus the sibling `rests on a listing entry`), `suspect: competing slot-filler named in a Searched outcome never tested` (354), `schema integrity: constraint hits not consumed` (357) and `suspect: sibling work named by a cited document never tested` (377). They cannot fire on this class BY CONSTRUCTION, and the data says why. The failures are not mis-adjudications of a candidate that was in hand: the GOLD ANSWER STRING appears in only 2 of the 20 deliverables (18/20 never name it anywhere in matrix, chain or answer line), so there was never a rival to adjudicate - this is candidate-FORMATION loss, not selection loss. The funnel: 13/20 retrieved a gold-bearing doc, only 6/13 CITED it (the passing control cites the expected doc in 22/26 = 85%), and 0 shipped it. The rules are blind to this because (a) they judge what the deliverable DECLARES - grounding checks the shipped value, which is attested, just not decisive; (b) the auditor's tooling reaches only CITED chunks and line 354d explicitly forbids hunting omitted competitors ("you cannot re-run the Searched calls"); (c) line 377's widening is scoped to "the documents already in the deliverable" and to sibling WORKS, so a gold passage sitting in an uncited retrieved doc (7 of the 13) is unreachable, and a different filler of the asked slot inside a chunk of a cited doc is out of its scope. WHAT TO BUILD, in order: (1) instrument per-doc reads (read_docids) - today only counts are logged (q1021 deep-read 458 chunks, no record of which docs), so "read then silently dropped" cannot be told from "never read"; (2) a MECHANICAL gate precheck on the sets the run already has: a doc that was deep-read yet appears in no Tested/Retained/Eliminated line, while carrying passages that match the question's rarest terms, fails as `read_but_uncited` and must be cited or dismissed with a reason - this is the only check that can see a candidate that never entered the text (narrow it to deep-read docs: 224 docs were merely retrieved for q1021, so retrieval alone is too coarse); (3) widen line 377 from sibling works to any different filler of the asked slot attested in a chunk of a CITED document, using the number_neighbors widening it already mandates. Also corrected here: q3 shipped the gold in the newest run and had been left in the failed bucket - moved to passed (520 -> 521).

history._read_but_uncited_viability_20260915: IS A read_but_uncited CHECK VIABLE? Measured 2026-09-15 and answered NO for every cheap form. The ledger's discriminating quantity is 'the uncited chunk holds the gold string' (q297 7 against 0 and 0 for the two questions that passed) - and that is a POST-HOC label, not a signal a gate can read. Every mechanical proxy was measured on the same three rows and none separates the outcomes: raw uncited chunk count (fail 43 vs pass 62 and 1); uncited chunks containing one of the question's anchor terms (18 vs 55 and 1 - the PASSING run fires three times harder); uncited chunks carrying a name the deliverable never mentions (43 vs 61 and 1); documents opened and never cited as a share of documents opened (fail 36/43 = 84% vs pass 21/26 = 81% and 1/9 = 11%). The reason is structural, not noise: reading far more than the deliverable uses is the NORMAL state of this pipeline - the passing q575 deep-read 67 chunks and cited 5 - so a check on unused reading fires hardest on the runs that did best, and the same trap closed the earlier attempt at bookkeeping enforcement (unrecordedLocateTools hit 69% of 703 rows and was therefore kept as diagnosis only). The one remaining version - have the auditor read the uncited set and judge whether a passage in it holds the answer - pays 43-62 chunk deep-reads on EVERY question for a yield that is conditional, so it is not worth its always-on cost. CONCLUSION: keep the ledger as a diagnostic (it earned its keep by settling the mechanism) and do NOT build a read-but-uncited gate. Caveat: n=3 (1 fail, 2 pass); the control run of four known passers (outputs/browsecomp_ctl4, seed 20260915: 263/550/836/8) was still in flight when this was written and can only strengthen the 'passing runs also read far more than they use' half of it.

history._gold_string_is_not_attestation_20260915: METHOD CAVEAT for every chunk-ledger verdict: 'a chunk containing the gold STRING was read' is NOT 'the answer was attestable from what the model read'. Found while analysing q297: its 4 gold-bearing chunks are all incidental mentions of the film title - a filmography line in another film's article, a retrospective aside, and a top-ten listing entry ('Insomnia2 of 10 Insomnia (2002)') - none of which states the property the question asks about, so 'gold_read_never_cited' described a title string rather than the answer. The effect is strongest when the gold is a common word or a title that appears in enumerations (q297's 'Insomnia' occurs in 214 corpus docs), and it is the same distinction the auditor contract already draws for candidates: a listing, bibliography or catalogue line names a thing and states nothing about it. USE THE VERDICT AS A HYPOTHESIS, NOT A CONCLUSION: when it says 'read', INSPECT the retrieved passage before attributing the loss to candidate formation; when it says 'never read', the reachability probe (class + gold_rank) tells whether a name query would have found it, which is what separates 'unreachable' from 'one name away'.
history._eih_mechanism_classification_20260915: MECHANISM CLASSIFICATION OF failed_evidence_in_hand, completed 2026-09-15 on the 17-question run (outputs/browsecomp_eih_all, wall 8354s): 1 passed (872), 16 failed. The ledger's verdicts, EACH INSPECTED against the retrieved text (the q297 lesson: a gold string in a chunk is not an attestation), split the failures into five mechanisms with different remedies: (1) gold_never_read, 10 of 16 - 223/233/323/561/873/909/794/898/1236/1232; (2) candidate formation (attestation read, never cited), 1 - 618; (3) the cited passage was a LISTING/title/incidental mention rather than an attestation, 3 - 293/297/1021; (4) the evidence is not in the index at all, 1 - 912; (5) the gold string is absent from its own evidence set, 1 - 1193. TWO CONTROLS make the dominant class trustworthy. First, indexing is NOT the cause: of the 47 expected documents across all 17 questions, 46 hold 88-152% of their corpus file's text in ES (over 100% is chunk overlap) and only q912's single document is under-indexed (1395 of 13840 characters), so the 10 never-read cases had their content indexed and simply never retrieved it. Second, reachability: the family is usually one name away. Also noted: the ledgers verdict and the grade disagreed on exactly the three listing/incidental cases (293, 297 and 1021 report a gold chunk read or cited, yet failed because what was read or cited does not attest the answer) - which is why the classification required inspection rather than a threshold. All five inspected runs shipped WITHOUT a concluding PASS audit (last-round suspects 5-13), i.e. best-effort deliveries after failed repairs. NEXT ACTION the data supports: 10 of 16 failures are the retrieval/hypothesis line (query the answer family by name), 1 is formation discipline, 3 are producer repair capability, and 2 are not the pipeline's fault at all (one ingest anomaly, one annotation mismatch).

RESULT: 85 complete, 5 with the index holding only a SUBSET of the file, 22 that differ from the file in both directions and 23 partially overlapping. The 5 content losses are 33637 (8% of the file present), 34297 (41%), 64576 (43%), 11992 (57%) and 7850 (63%); a wildcard check confirmed no second document carries the rest, so for these sources the ingest extracted only part of the file - and q912, whose ONLY expected document is 33637, is therefore not a pipeline failure at all. The 22/23 differ-both-ways documents are table/filmography reflows (the index flattens `| k = v` tables and the file keeps them), where both directions gap by similar amounts and nothing is lost. NO document is hidden from list_chunks: the available_int filter hides nothing in this corpus. FOUR TRAPS this sweep had to survive, each of which produced a wrong answer first: (1) character windows reported ~90% coverage for complete documents because their gaps sat on MediaWiki markup the ingest rewrites - word n-grams are immune; (2) reading available_int == 1 as an equality marked every chunk of a document invisible, while the engine actually translates it to must_not range(available_int < 1), which keeps chunks whose flag is ABSENT (elasticsearch/chunk.go:2058-2082); (3) a single-direction metric cannot tell a dropped section from a reflowed table - the ASYMMETRY between the two directions is the signal; (4) match_phrase on content_with_weight returns zero hits for phrases known to be present, and match on content_ltks matches a million chunks, so neither is a presence test - the only sound test is fetching every chunk of the document, which this script does. Questions whose evidence is materially incomplete: {"851": ["7850"], "869": ["34297"], "26": ["11992", "64576"], "912": ["33637"]}.
history._reparse_experiment_20260915: RE-PARSE EXPERIMENT on the 27 documents the coverage sweep flagged (5 content_missing_from_index + 22 index_and_file_differ), 2026-09-15. RESULT: coverage is UNCHANGED by a fresh parse, so the shortfall is a deterministic property of the ingest path, not an indexing accident. 33637 8.2%->8.2%, 34297 41.2%->41.3%, 64576 42.7%->42.7%, 11992 57.0%->57.0%, 7850 62.7%->62.7%, and all 22 differ-in-both-directions documents identical to the digit (only chunk counts moved: 130->147, 133->144, 245->261). SOURCE VERIFIED: document.location is 34297.md / 33637.md and document.size matches the corpus file byte for byte, so the index was built from the very file the benchmark calls the reference. MECHANISM EVIDENCE: the loss is interleaved, not a prefix - in 34297's single 194,395-character line the text is present in the index at offsets 0/5k/150k and absent at 20k/50k/100k/190k, and the corpus files carry extremely long unbroken lines (194k/178k/116k characters in 34297), which points at the chunker's handling of very long unbroken lines rather than at any truncation limit. A character-window or prefix/suffix model does not fit the data. OPERATIONAL INCIDENT worth remembering: re-parsing is a QUEUE operation - the API deletes the old chunks and publishes the task to NATS JetStream, and this deployment runs only --admin and --api, so with no --ingestor consuming the stream all 27 documents ended up with run=3 (DONE) and chunk_num=0: the partial evidence they HAD was gone. Starting bin/ragflow_server --ingestor drained the queued tasks and re-parsed all 27 (KB empty-document count back to 0); the ingestor is now running. Never trigger a re-parse on this deployment without an ingestor up, and prefer stopping it again afterwards if parse work is not wanted. CONSEQUENCE for the failure analysis: q912 (whose only expected document is 33637) cannot be won by any retrieval change, and the retrieval_strategy questions that depend on these documents (26, 851, 869) stay confounded until the corpus is re-ingested in a way that keeps the text.
history._markdown_text_loss_fix_20260915: TWO text-loss bugs in the Go markdown parser's text walker (internal/parser/parser/markdown_parser.go, leafText/walkLeaf), found by chasing why 33637.md indexed 8% of its file. (1) markdownNew() built its parser from parser.CommonExtensions, which includes MathJax, so every `$...$` span became an ast.Math node whose payload lives on the node literal rather than in a child Text node - and walkLeaf did not handle it, deleting the span. 33637.md, a financial report with 12 '$', parsed 13,840 characters down to 1,393; a file whose two '$' are far apart loses everything in between. (2) walkLeaf also ignored ast.HTMLSpan, the node for raw inline HTML glued to prose (a <table> with no blank line around it): 34297.md, 664k characters, lost 397,166 of them across 14 such spans. FIX: mask MathJax off in markdownNew() (Python's markdown library has no math extension, so '$' stays literal text and the two parsers agree) and emit the payloads of ast.Math / ast.MathBlock / ast.HTMLSpan in walkLeaf. Regression tests TestMarkdownParser_ParseWithResult_DollarIsCurrencyNotMath and _InlineRawHTMLSurvives. After the fix the Go parser matches Python: 33637 -> 13,833 characters over 3 items (13,839 over 2 sections on the Python side). VERIFIED in production after ./build.sh --go plus an ingestor restart: 34297 41.2%->99.9% (130->368 chunks), 64576 42.7%->99.7% (133->346), 11992 57.0%->99.8% (245->431), 7850 62.7%->100.0% (29->47); 33637 re-queued in the same pass. CORPUS-WIDE IMPACT, measured by replaying the old walker over the corpus: 8,398 of 67,707 files (12.4%) had lost text, 27,893,873 characters (1.4% of the corpus); more than 5% lost in 680 files, more than 25% in 126, more than 50% in 36. The affected list is outputs/markdown_text_loss_docs.json and the re-parse is driven by scripts/browsecomp_reparse_docs.py (resumable, state in ~/.cache/browsecomp_reparse_state.json, log outputs/reparse_loss_docs.log); all 8,398 were queued on 2026-09-15 16:05. LESSON for the coverage work: the markdown chunker and the Go TokenChunker were both verified lossless on this file - the loss was entirely in the parser's text walker, which is why a re-parse with the same parser reproduced the shortfall exactly.
history._embedding_ratelimit_and_reparse_2026091: EMBEDDING RATE LIMIT. The corpus embedding model is SiliconFlow bge-m3 behind a TPM quota, and it answered 429 Too Many Requests ("TPM limit reached") while the 8,398-document re-parse ran with max_concurrent_workers raised from 2 to 8. The retry that existed in internal/ingestion/task/embedder.go waited only 2s/4s/8s/16s - about 30 seconds in total, which always expires inside one 60-second TPM window, so a large document (71357 is 2.2M characters, 95876 2.25M) could never win: sixteen documents ended FAILED with their chunks already deleted by the re-parse. FIX (embedder.go, siliconflow.go): the schedule is now 5s/10s/20s/40s/80s capped at 120s with +/-20% jitter (about 2.5 TPM windows of patience, 6 attempts), the SiliconFlow driver carries Retry-After in the error so the provider's own hint is honored when it sends one, and a cooldown registry damps ALL workers at once instead of each one retrying independently against the same exhausted quota. SCOPE MATTERS: the cooldown is keyed by provider instance (endpoint + region + model + hashed API key), never process-globally - a TPM quota belongs to the credentials, so a worker throttled on provider A must not stall ingestion through provider B - and it cannot hang off the embedder value either, because newEmbedderResolver builds a fresh embedder per tokenizer invocation (one per document), so per-value state would never be shared by the workers actually competing for the quota. Tests in internal/ingestion/task/embedder_ratelimit_test.go cover the retry, the give-up path, fail-fast on non-429, cooldown sharing within one provider instance, non-interference across provider instances, the quota-key derivation (no plaintext secret in the key) and the Retry-After parser. VERIFIED after ./build.sh --go plus an ingestor restart: zero 429 events in the log since, no new FAILED task (16 pre-existing ones still need the retry pass), throughput 16 docs/min, 6,580 of 8,398 documents left (~7 hours). The Python tokenizer already treats 408/429 as retryable (rag/llm/embedding_model.py _batched_encode), so the two paths agree again. NATS CONSUMER SELF-HEAL GAP, found while doing this: killing and restarting the ingestor inherits the previous process's ephemeral JetStream consumer, which works for a few minutes and then gets reclaimed by NATS, after which every fetch fails with 'nats: no responders available for request' forever and the queue stops draining (6,550 tasks sat SCHEDULED in MySQL, 16 nodes started and 0 finished). The consumer is only created at startup, so the process cannot recover on its own; a second restart - now that the orphan is gone - fixes it, which is what was done. Worth a code fix: recreate the consumer when Fetch returns no-responders, and prefer a durable consumer name so restarts do not orphan one. REPARSE DRIVER: scripts/browsecomp_reparse_docs.py now reports completion by chunk_num (a queued document also reads run=3 with chunk_num=0, so run cannot distinguish queued from finished) and gained --retry-failed, which re-queues documents whose LATEST ingestion_task is FAILED - document.chunk_num is not a valid failure signal because a queued document has zero chunks too.
history._nats_consumer_selfheal_20260915: NATS CONSUMER SELF-HEAL. A restarted ingestor could end up pulling against a consumer handle that no longer addressed a live consumer, and every fetch then answered 'nats: no responders available for request' forever: the workers logged errors, the queue stopped draining (6,550 tasks sitting SCHEDULED in MySQL, 16 started and 0 finished), and only yet another restart cleared it. The consumer already had a fixed durable name (RAGFLOW_CONSUMER), so the fix is about the handle, not the name: internal/engine/nats/nats.go now classifies consumer-gone errors - typed jetstream.ErrConsumerNotFound / ErrConsumerDeleted / nats.ErrNoResponders first, with a string fallback - rebuilds the consumer and retries the pull a bounded number of times (5 attempts, 200ms apart), so a persistent failure still surfaces instead of spinning. Two details mattered: the error arrives through messages.Error() as often as through Fetch's return value, so both paths feed the classification (an earlier version that only guarded Fetch never triggered the repair, which is how the bug hid); and a pull issued in the instant after the consumer is created can land before the server registers the new pull subject, which is why the repair retries instead of declaring failure. The handle is now guarded by a mutex because the pull loop and the admin inspection endpoint share one engine. Tests: internal/engine/nats/consumer_selfheal_test.go (error classification, repair actually delivers new tasks afterwards, and a healthy empty pull leaves the handle alone) - the repair test deletes the consumer behind the engine's back and asserts that a pull stops erroring and that newly published tasks flow again. NOTE ON WHAT RECOVERY COVERS: the task stream is Retention=WorkQueuePolicy, so messages pending for a deleted consumer are gone with it - recreating the consumer restores the pull plumbing, it does not resurrect those messages. Also left alone on purpose, pre-existing on HEAD: TestInitMigratesLegacyStreamConfig fails (MaxBytes after migration = 1073741824, want 67108864) - unrelated to this change. VERIFIED: rebuild plus restart gives zero no-responders errors and 34 task starts in the first minute.
history._mysql_ingestion_tuning_20260915: MYSQL BOTTLENECK. mysqld was the busiest process on the box (141% CPU) and it was capping the 8,398-document re-parse at 23.5 documents/minute. performance_schema said where the time went: COMMIT averaged 68.2ms over 211,960 commits (14,388 seconds of MySQL CPU, the single largest consumer) because innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit=1 plus sync_binlog=1 forced two fsyncs per transaction, and the buffer pool was 128MB against 186MB of document data alone; the second consumer was a document-scheduling poll (SELECT ... process_begin_at, parser_config, progress_msg, run FROM document WHERE status=? AND NOT type=? AND (run IS NULL OR run!=?) AND (progress range OR id IN (SELECT doc_id FROM task ...))) that had run 17,870 times, examined 1,298,898,820 rows (72,686 rows per call - a full scan every time) at 467ms a call. Applied live, without a restart, since all of these are dynamic in 8.0.40: innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit=2, sync_binlog=0, innodb_buffer_pool_size=4G, innodb_io_capacity=2000 (the disk is NVMe), innodb_io_capacity_max=4000, innodb_redo_log_capacity=1G. MEASURED RESULT, same load: COMMIT 68.2ms -> 1.62ms, ingestion 23.5 -> 55.9 documents/minute (2.4x), and the monitoring queries that took 3s now take ~0.24s. ETA for the remaining 7,000 documents went from ~4.9 hours to about 2. Persisted as mysqld flags in docker/docker-compose-base.yml so a container restart keeps them (SET GLOBAL alone would not survive). TRADE-OFF, recorded deliberately: with flush_log_at_trx_commit=2 and sync_binlog=0 a HOST-level crash can lose up to one second of committed transactions (progress bookkeeping tolerates that); restore the two durable defaults if the database itself must be strictly durable. Still open, in expected-value order: (1) the scheduling poll still full-scans document ~10 times a minute at ~330ms - an index on (status, run) would cut it to a few hundred rows; (2) ingestion_task_log has grown to 802,131 rows (135MB data + 184MB index) from one row per progress event, so pruning or writing fewer events would pay off; (3) the sink-batching idea is now DEPRIORITIZED - at 1.62ms per commit the 5,267 commits per three minutes cost about 8.5 seconds, i.e. ~5% of a core; (4) the coverage tooling's own queries (SELECT id, run, chunk_num FROM document WHERE kb_id=?) also showed up at 3s per call and were part of the load.
history._mysql_followup_index_and_log_prune_2026: MYSQL FOLLOW-UP, both items the tuning left open. (1) INDEX FOR THE SCHEDULING POLL: does not exist as an option - the two candidate indexes are already present (idx_document_run and idx_document_progress) and MySQL ignores both for this query, which still examines 72,686 rows (a full document scan) per call at ~190ms. The predicate is an OR of a progress range, an id IN (subquery on task) and another progress/run/subquery combination, so no single-column index is usable; the poll runs ~10-20 times a minute from an EXTERNAL Python deployment (connections arrive from 172.18.0.1, i.e. the host, and from 192.168.1.24 on the LAN, both as root against the published port), i.e. it is DocumentService.get_unfinished_docs() in api/db/services/document_service.py. The realistic remedies are therefore (a) stop or throttle that Python scheduler, which is an environment decision, or (b) make that query index-friendly on the Python side. NOTE for whoever keeps it running: a second, Python-side RAGFlow polling the same MySQL can also schedule documents, so it competes with the Go ingestor - worth checking that it is not parsing behind our back. (2) ingestion_task_log PRUNING: 822,839 rows, of which 764,920 (93%) came from the original 24-26 August ingest and nothing at all was written between 27 August and 15 September. Deleted everything older than 7 days in 39 batches of 20,000 (with a short pause between batches), leaving 58,486 rows. Space stays inside the tablespace for reuse; OPTIMIZE TABLE would return it to the OS and was skipped because it rebuilds the table while ingestion is live. COMBINED RESULT: mysqld has gone from the busiest process on the box (141.8% CPU) to 4.7%, ingestion is at 5,309 of 8,398 documents with ~20-25 documents/minute and about 2.5 hours left, and the MySQL side is no longer a constraint at all.
history._es_bulk_refresh_parity_20260915: ES BULK REFRESH, the second item of the Tokenizer follow-up. The ingestion path wrote chunks with Refresh=wait_for (internal/engine/elasticsearch/chunk.go), which against the KB index's refresh_interval=1000ms means every bulk write waited for a refresh: measured median 507ms per write (p90 1039ms). That wait buys nothing during ingestion - the index publishes the chunks on its own refresh cycle a second later - and it is also a parity deviation: Python's ingestion inserts with refresh=False (rag/svr/task_executor_refactor/chunk_service.py:386 and :423) while its API default stays wait_for. FIX: InsertChunks now delegates to an internal insertChunks(refresh) and a new InsertChunksNoRefresh omits the parameter entirely (empty means the go-elasticsearch client drops it, so the index decides); the ingestion writer picks the no-refresh variant through an optional interface so engines that do not implement it keep the old path. Tests: internal/engine/elasticsearch/chunk_refresh_test.go asserts the plain inserter still sends wait_for and the ingestion inserter omits the parameter. MEASURED after rebuild and restart: ES bulk write median 507ms -> 288ms in the 20:00 bucket (a tighter window measured 136ms; the pairing heuristic is noisy with eight concurrent writers, so treat the range as ~140-290ms rather than a single figure). IMPORTANT NON-FINDING, recorded so nobody misreads the same numbers: the Tokenizer stage median rose from ~2.9s to ~9.1s, but the step happened at 19:30, half an hour BEFORE this change was deployed, with zero 429 events and unchanged chunks per document (~27-40) - that is embedding-service latency drifting, not a regression from removing the refresh wait. It matches the conclusion already recorded for the Tokenizer: the embedding service is the dominant and least controllable term.
history._concurrency_scaling_recheck_20260915: CONCURRENCY SCALING RE-CHECK, after the MySQL tuning and the ES refresh change moved the bottlenecks. Previous verdict (8 -> 12 workers gave nothing) was taken while MySQL was the wall and the box sat at load 15; the conditions had changed, so it was re-measured. Current state first: all eight workers busy, 15.6 documents/minute, and the per-stage plumbing overhead that used to cost ~0.35s per stage now costs 0.03-0.08s (File 0.03s, Parser 0.04s, Chunker 0.08s, Extractor 0.03s) - the MySQL tuning removed it, which is why the Tokenizer is now essentially the whole document: median 10.66s, mean 20.35s, end to end median 10.95s. Load average was 3.72 on 16 cores with no 429s, so the box was no longer CPU-bound and the test was worth running. RESULT AT 16 WORKERS: 18.6 documents/minute against 15.6 at 8 - a 19% gain for a doubling of concurrency - while the Tokenizer's own duration doubled with it (median 10.66s -> 19.50s, mean 20.35s -> 26.40s, p90 49.50s). That is the signature of a saturated upstream: the embedding service absorbs added client concurrency as latency instead of throughput, so elasticity to concurrency is roughly 0.19 and per-document resource holding time doubles for a marginal gain. CONCLUSION: raising concurrency cannot meaningfully raise throughput here - the embedding service (SILICONFLOW, TPM-quota'd) is the wall, exactly as suspected; the only levers that would move it are a larger quota or a local embedding model. 16 workers were left in place because they are still slightly faster and neither CPU (load 6.4/16) nor the quota (0 x 429) complained, but nothing beyond 16 is worth trying. Remaining work at that point: 2,288 documents, about two hours.

【桶定义，2026-09-21 定案；均为 annotations 下的键】
六桶**两两无交集**、合计 = 全量 830（当前各桶题数见 `_summary`）：
  passed                    = **自动判分**判对的题。
  failed_corpus_unanswerable = **语料不可答**：问题的 gold（或其区分性成分）在本语料里根本不存在（全语料 0 命中），因此无论检索/推理多好都不可能答对 ⇒ 评估时应从"系统缺陷"里扣除。
  passed_suspicious_judge   = 人工/代理复核判定为**对**、但判定不来自可信自动判分的题（判分器判错而复核认为对；或判分提供方拒判后人工裁定）。**与 passed 互斥**：判定来源是人工，故不计入 passed（与 q744 最初那条规则统一）。
  failed_retrieval_strategy = 判错且 recall=0（gold 证据一条都没被召回）。
  failed_evidence_in_hand   = 判错且 recall>0（期望证据已召回但答案仍错，含值槽写放弃声明/撤回答案）。
  failed_suspicious_judge   = 判分口径不可信、**待复核**的队列（复核后按结论迁出到上面各桶，故当前为空）。
**台账铁律**：一题只属一个桶；进任何 failed_* 桶即从 passed 移除；passed_suspicious_judge 与 passed 亦互斥。
复核结论的**权威存储**是 `annotations.verdict_overrides`（id → verdict/bucket/grounds）与 `annotations.gold_overrides`（标注缺陷修正）。
筛子判据（分诊用，可生成待复核队列）：取 Final/Guessed Answer 行的槽位值（剥离 (assumption:…)/(tie:…)）、非放弃措辞、两侧含字母 token；命中任一：① gold ⊆ 值 且 gold 占值 ≥50% ② 值 ⊆ gold 且值占 gold ≥40% ③ 相似度 ≥0.8 且两侧 ≤10 token。⚠️ 自动筛子**只分诊、不加分**：实测排空后 precision 仅 0/3，必须人工/代理裁定。
【failed_corpus_unanswerable 定界流程（2026-09-21 定案，可复用）】对候选题按下列三条逐词元判定（源文件层面，不依赖 ES；工具：全语料 `rg -l -i -F`）：

  ③ 词元在参考文档里、但 ES chunk 文本没有 ⇒ 入库丢词（**本轮 0 例**）。
  本轮扫描：候选 15 题（来源＝参考文档缺词元 ∪ full-gold 串不在语料）→ ①**1 题（q253）**、②1 题（q406，实为 gold 笔误 'Masata'→'Masato'，已按标注缺陷修正并判对）、③0 题、其余 13 题 OK。
